toc.title: Not everyone you call a friend is the same
Challenging is not the same as draining

blocks.p: This topic comes up a lot in my work with teenagers, and in my work with adults as well: friendships and relationships, healthy boundaries, and what your obligations and responsibilities are. How much of yourself do you want to give? I want to help you get some clarity on that and put your energy where it needs to be.

blocks.h: Not everyone you call a friend is the same

blocks.p: This is about the people in your life. It doesn't have to be just friends. It could be family or relatives, pretty much anyone. We can bring a new lens to all of them.

The people you're calling friends: maybe they are friends, but are they really? There might be people in your life you call friends who are draining for you, or who aren't adding value to your life. I'm not talking about financial value. Maybe they're energy suckers, energy vampires. There might be people in your life you feel safe and connected around, who are fulfilling. There might be people who are energizing. To call all of these people friends is fine, but there could be different levels of friendship. So how do we conceptualize the people in our life?

This might sound really distasteful, so I'll just put it out there: how do we rank the people in our lives? I know that sounds horrible. Put it this way: how do we rank how much energy we give to the people in our life? Or, how do we categorize the relationships we have, and where do the people in our life fit into them?
Here's the way I typically break it down.

ul: Best friends. The people closest to us. Even as adults, we can have best friends. That's maybe one or two people. It might be your spouse, and if it is, good for you. These are the people who help fulfill you as an individual.

Friends. Close, but not that core. You spend time together and share some level of emotional connection, probably a pretty good amount, and you can't imagine life without them. These might also be people you drift away from as you get older, but they are your friends in the present moment.

Acquaintances. People you chit-chat with at work, maybe have lunch with, maybe share some personal stuff with, but for the most part it's professional or friendly. You can live without them. You'll be okay. They may be temporary, based on the context of your life. You're not going to put energy into seeing them outside of work or school. You say hi and chit-chat.
Neutral. People you pass by. They don't add value to your life, and they don't take anything away. They don't give energy, and they don't take energy. Passersby on the street.
Harmful or toxic. People who are an active hindrance to your life, and to how you feel about yourself. I know nowadays everybody's narcissistic. I get it. Maybe we'll put them here.

blocks.h: Challenging is not the same as draining

blocks.p: This is where we have to be careful, because the people who are maybe the best for us are also challenging. They're loving, but they're challenging. So you'll have to discern: is this my spouse, who loves the heck out of me and is challenging me? Or is this someone who's a life suck, draining me, maybe for their own fulfillment? Regardless of the other person's motivation, check in with how you feel around them, and be honest with yourself.

You can also be honest with yourself and say that you have friends you love the heck out of, who are good for you and you're good for them, and you just don't want to hang out with them right now. You can't. You're done for the day. You're checked out. Maybe the morning was too much. That doesn't mean they're passersby in your life. It just means you don't have anything left to give. They're still your friends. That's different from someone you dread being around, who drains you of your energy.

One of my clients, a high schooler, called this his six rings of friendship. I think I've given you five, but he had six. I think it had something to do with Lord of the Rings, the rings of power maybe. It was a nerdier reference.

That clicked for him. Conceptualizing things this way really helped him decide: where do I want to put my energy? Are there people on a certain ring I want to bump up? Maybe there's someone on the friendship ring I want to make into a best friend, or invest more of myself in, because I feel the other person is inviting it, or giving it to me, and I want to match them where they're at. Or you put yourself out there, and if they reject it, now you know.

So it might be possible to look at people who are really good for you, who you've maybe been keeping at the acquaintance level, and give them a little more of your energy. Obviously it has to be reciprocated, so you'll have to try things out and see where it goes.
The immediate thing you can do is put less energy and less time into the people who are lower down on your rings of friendship. That's where you can start.
There might be some people, especially in that toxic ring, who you do have to cut out. That's what's best for you, and you just have to be honest with yourself about it.

I know categorizing people sounds horrible. Call it your rings of friendship, or whatever you want to call it. Make it palatable for you. I don't know how else to put it without it sounding objectifying, but this is the reality of it. When it comes to this stuff, you have to be kind of starkly honest, and whenever I do this with people, it seems to help them a lot.

As you set up your rings, you might notice, "Oh, I'm putting a lot of energy into ring three, and I really should be putting it more into ring one." And by the way, ring one might be yourself. You might be at the core of it.
